analysis.one_liner: Extends the Children's Health Insurance Program and lowers out-of-pocket costs for low-income families' kids.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have kept federal funding for the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) flowing through fiscal 2019 at set levels, created a fund to bail out states that run short of CHIP money, and capped what families pay in premiums and copays under Medicaid and CHIP at 5% of income. It also would have made preventive care and vaccines free for children and pregnant women, automatically enrolled newborns in CHIP, and made it easier for families to move between Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace plans without losing coverage. It never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income children and pregnant women covered by CHIP or Medicaid. The bill extended CHIP funding through FY2019 [S2][S3], created a CHIP Shortfall Fund so states that run out of money could keep kids covered [S2][S3], capped family cost-sharing at 5% of income [S2][S3], banned cost-sharing on pregnancy-related and preventive care and new vaccines [S2][S3], and let states extend CHIP to children with special health care needs up to age 26 [S2][S3]. It also would have automatically enrolled newborns and made it easier for kids in immigrant and foster families to enroll [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Extends CHIP funding through fiscal year 2019 with annual allotments of roughly $19-21 billion and a $16.7 billion one-time appropriation, plus a $3.86 billion CHIP Shortfall Fund to cover states that would otherwise run out of money.
Caps total annual premiums, enrollment fees, and cost-sharing under Medicaid and CHIP at 5% of family income, with tracking, suspension of charges once the cap is hit, and notification to families.
Eliminates cost-sharing for preventive services for children and pregnant women and requires coverage of newly approved vaccines within 30 days of federal recommendation.
Automatically enrolls newborns in CHIP, makes the Express Lane and outreach grant programs permanent, and lets states extend CHIP to children with special health care needs up to age 26.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill appropriated billions from the Treasury without offsetting revenue: about $21 billion for FY2015 and roughly $19-21 billion annually through FY2019, a $3.86 billion shortfall fund, $750 million per year in performance bonuses, and $400 million per year for home visiting programs [S3]. States choosing new options would also face administrative costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill committed tens of billions of dollars in new federal spending over five years without a funding offset, adding to the deficit in a period when CHIP's future financing was actively debated.

Many of the biggest coverage improvements - a 5% cost-sharing cap, higher income eligibility, extended age limits - were state options rather than federal requirements, so the benefit to families would have varied widely by state.
The bill layered new enrollment, language-service, and cost-tracking duties on states and on Medicaid managed care insurers, with federal reimbursement for some but not all of the added cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and well-targeted: continued health coverage for millions of low-income kids and a real cap on what their families can be charged. The cost is substantial federal spending, and the design dilutes the benefit by making many protections optional for states. Still, CHIP has historically been one of the cheaper ways to cover children, and the bill's main purpose - keeping a program with broad bipartisan history funded - is the kind of spending most health economists consider high-value. The design is not perfect, but the tradeoff favors families over cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jay Rockefeller introduced the CHIP Extension Act of 2014 on June 11, 2014.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was taken - no subcommittee consideration, markup, or floor vote - before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody visibly gained. Low-income families got nothing from the bill's promised protections, and its death raised no concentrated interest's fortunes; the existing CHIP program simply continued on prior funding. The bill failed by inaction rather than by any organized opposition shown in the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the program ran on as before

for.name: Sen. Jay Rockefeller
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full extension, financing, and cost-sharing package in his final Congress.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and committee with jurisdiction over CHIP and Medicaid
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee but never scheduled a markup or advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator besides the sponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknowable from the record.

industries.note: The bill extends CHIP funding and adds enrollment, so managed care plans covering these kids would gain revenue and more enrollees. The new tracking and language-service duties would add compliance costs, but the headline effect is more business.

industries.industry: Pediatricians, dentists, and children's health providers
industries.note: Continued CHIP funding and coverage of preventive services and vaccines mean more insured young patients and fewer uncompensated visits. Extended dental cost-sharing limits also steer more families toward dental coverage.
